prospect.name: Giovanni Sornatale
prospect.occupation: Self-employed photographer with international commissions; just returned from a six-week project in Italy. Starts work at noon daily. Previously worked as a chef.
prospect.family_status: Married; he and his wife are considering having children in the next couple of years
prospect.training_background: Played a lot of sports in high school and has cycled in and out of fitness ever since, never sustaining more than two to three months and typically training toward a specific event such as his wedding. Currently trains with kettlebells unstructured — swings, single-arm swings, snatches, cleans, halos, bird dogs, push-ups and pull-ups — describing his own approach as 'I just pick up the kettlebell and see what happens'. Can hold a deep squat for several minutes and do four or five pull-ups. Solid kettlebell fundamentals by his own account and the rep's.

signals: Self-directed and genuinely capable — good kettlebell fundamentals, ex-athlete, holds a deep squat, and explicitly believes he could do it himself: 'part of me feels like I can just put some time and effort into coming up with a relatively simple workout plan with the knowledge that I have'
Arrived with a firm and low budget anchor stated before any price was mentioned: 'I wouldn't want to spend much more than, you know, 100, 150 bucks a month'

Wants to buy the smallest increment first and expand only on proven value: 'I'm the type of person that would want to like be sold up as I go through it. If I can find value initially, then, you know, and build trust in the program, then I will buy in more.'
Not the_optimizer despite fitting on profile — the price is not read as a quality signal here, it is a barrier he negotiated downward, and he questioned the value of even $200 a month

goals.text: Get a structured, plug-and-play routine he does not have to think about each morning
Build functional strength, explicitly over aesthetics
Increase pull-ups from four or five to a higher number
Become more flexible, particularly through tight hips
Reach and record his peak lifetime strength before age-related decline — 'at the peak of my life, I was the strongest I could have been'
Be in the best shape he can be for having children in the next couple of years
Avoid pulling his back again, having done so in the last couple of years
Add some visible muscle — 'I'd like some vanity muscles' and to grow his chest
Break the lifelong cycle of getting in shape then declining, and sustain it permanently
Train entirely from home without driving across LA traffic to a gym or class
Own the knowledge to sustain it himself — 'I just want the knowledge and the ability to take credence over my own life'

pains.text: No structure — not knowing what the workout will be actively prevents him from training: 'not knowing what I'm going to do sometimes just prevents me from doing it'
Lifelong cycle of committing for two to three months then falling off, which he calls 'a sick cycle' followed by self-loathing
Attributes the falling off to 'general laziness'
Intermittent lower back pain from sitting too long or not bracing, which resolves when he trains his core consistently
Pulled his back within the last couple of years and does not want it to recur
Two months of heavy indulgence during a photography project in Italy — pizza, pasta, beer, champagne, cheese
Overeats by quantity rather than by food quality — 'my issue isn't the quality of the food, it's more the quantity'
Actively wants to reduce social media exposure, which conflicts with learning from Trevor's Instagram content
Can only see three months ahead in his work schedule, limiting his willingness to commit long term

objections.raw_quote: Yeah, I mean, I'm gonna have to think about it. But I think, I mean, it's, my thing is, is, like, I don't know if I need to spend $200 a month to get it.
objections.rep_response: Challenged the DIY premise reasonably — 'You're mentioning, like, set up your own schedule, workout routine. Isn't that something you've been trying to do for the last however long?' — and tested the value directly, getting 'it's certainly worth $200 a month'. He did not then run the rest of the play.

objections.raw_quote: part of me feels like I can just put some time and effort into coming up with, you know, a relatively simple workout plan with the knowledge that I have and go from there.
objections.rep_response: Addressed once by pointing out he had been trying and failing to do exactly that for years. The prospect conceded the point ('Yeah, absolutely') but immediately reframed it as a spending decision rather than a capability one, and the rep did not press further.

objections.raw_quote: I'm not going to make a $200 a month decision without talking to her about it. Chances are, yes, she's going to say yes, but I want to sit down and go over my options and go from there.
objections.rep_response: Asked whether the wife supports his health decisions, whether she knew about the call, and whether she knew he had been trying to get in shape. Then asked 'And what if she says no?', which the prospect rebuffed sharply: 'I don't know. This isn't a marriage therapy class. I'm just looking to you to get a little bit of workout information.' The rep backed off immediately and agreed to email information.

evidence: No payment taken and no payment link sent — the rep agreed to email information instead: 'Just send it to my email.'
Explicit deferral: 'I'm gonna have to think about it' and 'I'm going to go talk to my wife about it, you know, and we'll make the decision and go from there.'
Positive lean but conditional: 'I'll probably sign up and give it a shot for a month' and 'I might give it a month and see what happens'.

Timeline agreed: prospect said speaking to his wife 'shouldn't take much longer than today', and the rep summarised 'by the end of the day or tomorrow, we'll hear back from you and basically get you started or not.'
Counter-evidence: he confirmed the value proposition when tested — 'it's certainly worth $200 a month' — so the deferral is about process and spousal consultation, not about disbelief in the product.
The close rule was not applied: no link was sent and the verbal position was 'probably', explicitly conditional on a conversation with his wife.
outcome.next_step: Rep to email details of the Kettlebell University community; prospect to discuss with his wife the same day and revert by the end of the day or the following day.

notable.note: The most significant commercial finding in the batch. This prospect never heard the $6,000 price. Asked what one-to-one coaching costs, the rep said 'usually in a couple of thousands', and when the prospect checked directly — 'So $2,000 for six months?' — answered 'No, it goes a little bit higher' and added that it 'depends a little bit on how specific you would make it', implying scope-variable pricing that does not exist. The rep had asked for the prospect's budget first ('what's the range that you were expecting for yourself?', answered $100-150 a month) and then presented an entirely different product, Kettlebell University, at $2,000 a year or $200 a month. On profile this is a near-textbook ICP fit who was routed away from the flagship offer on the strength of a stated budget anchor.

quality.notes: Frequent inversion, including several exchanges where the rep's questions and the prospect's answers appear under the same label. Most consequential around 00:25:48 to 00:26:38, where the pricing exchange about the one-to-one programme alternates speakers within single labelled blocks; roles there were resolved from content and the reading is that the prospect asked 'So $2,000 for six months?' and the rep answered 'No, it goes a little bit higher.' Also inverted at 00:05:40 to 00:05:47, where the age, height and weight answers sit under the rep's label. Weight was given as a range, 'probably like 190 to 200 pounds', and is recorded as the 195 midpoint. Stray transcription artefacts appear throughout, including 'Cylentronic', 'use youBoer', and 'credences' for what is almost certainly 'credence'.
